how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Security camera installation bid calculator

How much should I charge to install security cameras?

There is no flat per-camera price, because the same eight-camera job can be two very different labor tickets. Eight cameras through an accessible attic is one job. Eight through masonry with a lift, longer runs, and a switch that has to be sized for the PoE load is several times the labor — before either quote has priced the storage the customer is actually paying for.

Open the free security camera bid calculator

What a per-camera price cannot see

Access and construction type. Accessible attic runs and masonry runs with a lift are not the same drop labor, even at the same cable length.

Storage math. Eight 4 MP cameras on H.265, recording continuously, use roughly 0.35 TB per day — about 10.4 TB for 30 days of retention before usable-space headroom. Quoting "30 days of storage" without doing that math is quoting a number the drives may not actually hold.

PoE budget and run length. A switch has a wattage budget the cameras have to fit inside, and Ethernet has a hard run-length limit. Both are pass/fail checks a per-camera price skips entirely.

A bid you can defend

  1. Price labor hours per drop by construction type, not a flat per-camera rate.
  2. Size storage from resolution, codec, camera count, and hours recorded per day, then check it against the drives actually being quoted.
  3. Check PoE load against the switch budget and flag any run past the Ethernet limit.
  4. Load the wage, then add overhead, and price = cost ÷ (1 − target margin) for a walk-away number.

The calculator does that arithmetic in your browser. It is not an ONVIF profile, a manufacturer specification, or a building, fire, or privacy-law ruling — bitrates are typical planning figures at 15 fps, not a guarantee any camera hits them.

Worked example

Eight 4 MP cameras on H.265, recording continuously for a 30-day retention target, need roughly 10.4 TB before usable-space headroom — a number many quotes skip entirely in favor of "whatever drive comes with the NVR." Separately, the actual drives a customer is willing to pay for may deliver fewer retention days than promised, and a switch sized for eight cameras' PoE draw is a different bill of materials than one sized for four. The calculator checks storage, PoE budget, and run length together, so the gap between "30 days quoted" and "30 days delivered" doesn't surface at the handover.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install security cameras?

There is no flat per-camera price. Eight cameras through an accessible attic is a different job from eight through masonry with a lift. This calculator prices the drops, the cable, the head end, and the labour from your own wage, burden, overhead, and margin, and gives a walk-away price to hold when a customer asks you to match a lower bid.

How many terabytes do I need for 30 days of recording?

It depends on resolution, codec, camera count, and hours recorded per day. Eight 4 MP cameras on H.265 recording continuously use about 0.35 TB per day, so 30 days needs roughly 10.4 TB before usable-space headroom. This calculator computes it and, separately, the retention the drives you actually buy will deliver — those are different numbers, and the gap is where a handover fails.

Is this a manufacturer specification or a code ruling?

No. Outputs are arithmetic on the numbers you enter. Bitrates are typical planning figures at 15 fps, not a guarantee any camera hits them — a scene full of moving foliage will exceed them. Nothing here is an ONVIF profile, a manufacturer specification, or a building, fire, or privacy-law ruling.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not electrical, engineering, code, security, privacy, legal, tax, or contracting advice, and it does not replace a licensed installer, a manufacturer's specification, or the authority having jurisdiction. Verify every figure against your own takeoff and equipment specifications before relying on it or submitting a bid.

For low-voltage and security installers

Security camera bid calculator

Price the drops, the cable, and the head end from your own wage and margin — and check the three things a camera bid gets wrong before it goes out: whether the drives hold the recording days you are quoting, whether the switch can power the cameras, and whether any run is past the Ethernet limit.

The system

What is being recorded, and for how long the customer was told it would be kept.

Motion-only share is a planning estimate. A camera facing a busy street or moving foliage will record far more of the day than one in a stockroom.

Power and cable

The two site facts that turn into a change order when they are found on install day.

Typical draw: fixed dome or turret 6 W, bullet with IR 9 W, bullet with heater 13 W, PTZ 25 W. Heaters raise the winter load on a budget that looked fine in July.

Labour

Hours per drop follows the construction type until you type your own number, which then wins.

Materials and margin

Margin is on revenue, not markup on cost. Quoting cost × 1.35 and calling it a 35% margin is a 26% margin.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    What this does, and what it does not

    Why "days the drives hold" is a separate number from "storage needed"

    The arithmetic asks for a figure like 10.4 TB. You can buy 8 TB or 12 TB, not 10.4, and once the filesystem and the recorder's overwrite headroom take their slice you keep about 90% of the label. Quoting 30 days and handing over a system that holds 11 is the most common failed handover in this trade, so both numbers are shown and the shortfall is named.

    Why the PoE check matters more than it looks

    A switch over its budget does not fail cleanly. It drops cameras intermittently, often months later when heaters come on, and every one of those is a callback the bid never priced. The tool flags anything over 80% of the budget, because a system at its ceiling has nothing left for the camera added next spring.

    Bitrates are planning figures

    Figures assume roughly 15 fps and typical scenes. H.265 is credited at half of H.264, and smart-codec modes conservatively rather than at the marketing number, because their saving only materialises on static scenes. A camera watching traffic or moving foliage will exceed these. Nothing here is a manufacturer specification or an ONVIF profile.

    This is not legal advice about recording

    Where cameras may point, whether audio may be recorded, signage, and how long footage may be kept are governed by law that varies by country, state, and sometimes by the room. This tool prices an install; it does not tell you whether the install is lawful.

    Common questions

    How much should I charge to install security cameras?

    There is no flat per-camera price. Eight cameras through an accessible attic is a different job from eight through masonry with a lift. This calculator prices the drops, the cable, the head end, and the labour from your own wage, burden, overhead, and margin, and gives a walk-away price to hold when a customer asks you to match a lower bid.

    How many terabytes do I need for 30 days of recording?

    It depends on resolution, codec, camera count, and hours recorded per day. Eight 4 MP cameras on H.265 recording continuously use about 0.35 TB per day, so 30 days needs roughly 10.4 TB before usable-space headroom. This calculator computes it and, separately, the retention the drives you actually buy will deliver — those are different numbers, and the gap is where a handover fails.

    Is this a manufacturer specification or a code ruling?

    No. Outputs are arithmetic on the numbers you enter. Bitrates are typical planning figures at 15 fps, not a guarantee any camera hits them — a scene full of moving foliage will exceed them. Nothing here is an ONVIF profile, a manufacturer specification, or a building, fire, or privacy-law ruling.

    How many cameras can one PoE switch power?

    It depends on the switch's rated budget and what each camera actually draws, not a fixed camera count. A fixed dome or turret with no heater is a light load at about 6 W; a bullet with IR climbs to about 9 W; add a heater for winter and it is closer to 13 W; a PTZ needs PoE+ and can pull 25 W. A switch with a 120 W budget — this calculator's example default — powering eight bullet cameras with heaters is already at 104 W, 87% of budget, before the recorder or a spare port are counted. That is over the 80% planning ceiling this calculator flags, because a switch at its rated ceiling has nothing left for the camera added next spring, and running over budget does not fail cleanly — it drops cameras intermittently, often months later when the heaters come on. Standard PoE (802.3af) delivers 15.4 W at the switch port; PoE+ (802.3at) delivers 30 W, which is why a 25 W PTZ needs a PoE+ port and a PoE+-capable switch, not a standard one.

vs-a-flat-per-camera-price.html.text:
← Security Camera Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-camera price

“$900 a camera, installed” is not a price for a security system — it is a price for one construction type and one camera wattage, quietly applied to every drop that gets called in.

What a flat per-camera price is

A flat per-camera price is the fastest way to quote a camera install over the phone: multiply the camera count by a number and read it back. Customers shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's quote will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one kind of job — usually fixed-dome or bullet cameras through an accessible attic, on a switch with headroom — and then reused for every site afterward, whether or not the next one is masonry, needs a lift, or is specifying PTZ cameras that need PoE+.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the camera count, resolution, codec, and recording mode, the retention days quoted and the drives you actually plan to buy, the PoE switch budget and each camera's draw, the construction type and cable run, whether a lift is required, and your camera, NVR, and switch hardware costs, plus your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, permit fee, and target margin. It prices the drops by construction type, checks the PoE budget and cable run against real limits, and returns the bid price, the cost floor, and the price per camera — for this job and this site, not a flat number for every install.

What a flat per-camera price doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same fee whether the drop is through an open attic or through masonry that takes twice the hours — and has no line for a lift day at all. Prices labour hours per drop by construction type (open, attic, finished, masonry, soffit), and adds a lift's hours only when the job needs one.
Has no line for the switch or hardware a PTZ or heated camera needs over a fixed dome, regardless of the extra draw or the pricier unit. Prices each camera's watts against the switch's PoE budget and flags when the load is over budget or over an 80% planning ceiling, before you commit to a switch.
Quotes the same cable allowance for a short interior run and a long exterior one, with no check against the 328 ft Ethernet limit. Prices cable footage with a waste allowance and flags any run past the Ethernet limit, so a mid-span switch or extender is in the scope, not a surprise.
Has no separate line for camera, NVR, or switch hardware — the count is the whole quote. Prices camera, NVR, switch, drive, and cable materials as their own lines, so a heavier hardware spec is never quoted at the light spec's invoice.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat per-camera price would have quoted the same job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two eight-camera jobs, one flat price

Using this calculator's own shipped starting example:

Eight fixed-dome cameras through an accessible attic, on a 120 W switch budget with headroom, prices at $7,440.38, on a job that costs $4,836.25 to run.

Take the same eight cameras and make them PTZ units through masonry instead — a lift for the runs, a PoE+ switch to carry the heavier draw, and longer cable to the exterior mounts — and the job costs $9,422.96 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator bids it at $14,496.86: 1.95 times the easy job, on the identical camera count. Quoting the masonry-and-lift job at the easy job's flat $7,440.38 price prices it $1,982.58 below its own break-even cost — before counting the $7,056.48 it falls short of this calculator's own bid price at a 35% target margin. Same camera count, same flat price, one site that pays and one that loses money the moment the lift shows up.

Common questions

Why does a flat per-camera price get a security camera install wrong?

Because the cost driver is the drop and the hardware, not the camera count. Eight fixed-dome cameras through an accessible attic need a straightforward pull and a light PoE budget. Eight PTZ cameras through masonry, with a lift for the runs and a PoE+ switch to carry the heavier draw, need roughly twice the labour hours and a materially larger hardware bill, on the same camera count. A flat per-camera price charges both the same because it was priced on the count, not the drop.

What does a flat per-camera price usually leave out entirely?

Construction type, a lift, and camera wattage. A flat price has no line for masonry drops that take twice the hours of an accessible attic, no line for a lift day when a run cannot be reached from a ladder, and no line for the heavier PoE+ switch and pricier hardware a PTZ or heated camera needs over a fixed dome. It also has no line for the longer cable runs an exterior or masonry job usually carries.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped starting example: eight fixed-dome cameras through an accessible attic, on a light PoE budget, prices at $7,440.38. The same eight cameras as PTZ units through masonry, with a lift, a PoE+ switch, and longer runs, cost $9,422.96 to complete and this calculator bids the job at $14,496.86 -- 1.95 times the easy job. Quoting the masonry-and-lift job at the easy job's $7,440.38 flat per-camera price prices it $1,982.58 below its own break-even cost, before a dollar of profit or the crew's time is covered, and $7,056.48 below this calculator's own bid.

Is a flat per-camera price ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- interior fixed-dome or bullet cameras through an accessible attic, on a switch with headroom -- a flat per-camera number can land close, because that is probably the job the price was set on. The risk is quoting a masonry job, a lift job, or a PTZ job the same way sight unseen, because the price does not know the construction type, the run length, or the camera wattage until someone walks the site, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or hardware costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market, your distributor's camera and switch pricing, or your permit fees. It takes the camera count, resolution, codec, construction type, cable run, camera wattage, drive and switch hardware, and your own wage, burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-camera price skips, not a market survey.

Open the Security Camera Bid Calculator to price your own job, or read the pricing walkthrough.

No warranty. This free tool is not electrical, engineering, code, security, privacy, legal, tax, or contracting advice, and it does not replace a licensed installer, a manufacturer's specification, or the authority having jurisdiction. Verify every figure against your own equipment, payroll, and site conditions before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against any competing service — it is a static page describing the calculator's own worked example.

Free and open source. If it wins you a job, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

This calculator vs. D-Tools

Two different shapes: D-Tools System Integrator is business-management software for running an AV, security, or low-voltage integration firm's whole design-to-delivery pipeline. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one camera install cost, and do the storage, PoE, and cable-run numbers on the quote actually hold up — before you send it.

What each tool is for

D-Tools makes System Integrator (SI), founded in 1998 by Adam Stone and headquartered in Concord, California. SI is business- management software purpose-built for AV, security, and low-voltage integrators: it connects system design (through an AutoCAD or Visio integration for engineered drawings), the bill of materials, procurement, project management, and financial visibility across a whole firm, with an on-premises edition and, since 2019, a cloud edition aimed at smaller projects. It is an account-based platform: a firm signs up and runs its design-to-delivery pipeline through it on an ongoing basis, not a one-off bid worksheet. D-Tools' own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — business-management and system-design software for the AV, security, and low-voltage integration trade — are stated, and no dollar amount for D-Tools appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what D-Tools does. It draws no CAD layout, tracks no procurement, and stores no customer or job record on a server.
